snp3.12:9.4: The term “acquisition” (upadhi), in its everyday sense, denotes the possessions, baggage, and other paraphernalia a nomadic family might carry in its wanderings; on the psychological level it denotes anything one has a sense of “I” or “mine” about, and so carries around as a kind of mental baggage. The verse following this prose passage is identical with the Buddha’s first answer to Mettagū at Sn 5:4.
snp3.12:33.3: Arousal translates ārambha, a word with several possible senses, among them disruption, seizure of an object, or the inception of action (often with violent connotations).
snp3.12:37.3: “There are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come into being or for the support of those in search of a place to be born. Which four? Physical food, gross or refined; contact as the second, intellectual intention the third, and consciousness the fourth.”—SN 12:63. For more, see SN 12:63–64.
snp3.12:53.2: “His release, being founded on truth, does not fluctuate, for whatever is deceptive is false; unbinding—the undeceptive—is true. Thus a monk so endowed is endowed with the highest determination for truth, for this—unbinding, the undeceptive—is the highest noble truth.”—MN 140
snp3.12:61.4: On Māra’s sway, see SN 4:19, SN 35:115, SN 35:189, and SN 35:199.
